Barefaced means doing something wrong — especially lying or cheating — openly, shamelessly, and without even trying to hide it.

When you call something "barefaced," you are saying two things at once:

  1. It is completely obvious to everyone around.
  2. The person doing it feels no shame or guilt about it whatsoever.

That combination — the total openness plus the total lack of shame — is exactly what makes "barefaced" such a powerful word.
The Heart of the Word: Shamelessness

The most important quality here is shamelessness. This isn't just about something being obvious. It's about someone being so bold in their wrongdoing that they don't even bother to hide it, deny it convincingly, or show any embarrassment.

Think of it this way. Imagine three people telling a lie:

  • Person A tells a careful, clever lie. They cover their tracks. They almost pull it off.
  • Person B tells a sloppy lie. They're not very good at it, and you can sort of see through it.
  • Person C looks you straight in the eyes, tells a complete lie, and doesn't even flinch — even when you know it's a lie, and they know you know.

Person C is telling a barefaced lie.

It is the lie told with a straight face and zero shame. That is the defining quality of "barefaced."
The Feeling It Creates in the Listener

When something is described as barefaced, the person using the word is almost always shocked or outraged. The word carries strong disapproval. It suggests that the behavior is not just wrong, but audaciously wrong — so open and unapologetic that it's almost hard to believe.

So when someone calls something "barefaced," they are not being neutral. They are saying: "Can you believe the nerve of this person?"
What "Barefaced" Is Almost Always Used To Describe

While the word can technically describe any shameless, undisguised wrongdoing, it is most commonly used with lies and deception. The phrase "a barefaced lie" is by far the most natural and frequent way to use this word. You will hear and read this combination constantly.

It can also describe:

  • A barefaced cheat — someone who cheats with no attempt to be subtle.
  • A barefaced attempt to do something dishonest or unfair.
  • Barefaced effrontery / audacity — shockingly bold and shameless behavior.

Here are clear, natural examples so you can see the word doing its job:

"He looked at the security camera footage of himself stealing and still told a barefaced lie to his manager's face."

"She made a barefaced attempt to take credit for her colleague's work in front of the entire team."

"I was stunned by the barefaced dishonesty of the salesman — he knew the product was faulty and said nothing."

"It was a barefaced lie, and everyone in the room knew it, including him."

Notice something in all these examples: the wrongdoing is visible, undeniable, and the person doing it isn't even properly embarrassed. That tension is always present.
How "Barefaced" Is Different from Similar Words

There are several words that are close in meaning but not identical. Understanding the differences will sharpen your understanding.

Barefaced vs. Blatant:
"Blatant" also means obvious and without shame. But "blatant" focuses more on the offensiveness of the act — how openly bad it is. "Barefaced" focuses more on the person's attitude — their lack of shame and their boldness. A blatant mistake can happen by accident; a barefaced lie is always deliberate.

Barefaced vs. Brazen:
"Brazen" is the closest word to "barefaced." Both describe shameless boldness. However, "brazen" is used more broadly — brazen behavior can be anything from rudeness to criminal acts. "Barefaced" is used more specifically with lies and deception, and carries a slightly stronger sense of shock that such a thing was done so openly.

Barefaced vs. Outright:
"An outright lie" means a complete, total lie with nothing true in it. "A barefaced lie" means a lie told with no shame or attempt to hide it. A lie can be outright but whispered guiltily — that would not be "barefaced." A barefaced lie is always bold and unashamed.
The Tone: When Do People Use This Word?

People reach for the word "barefaced" when they want to express moral outrage at how shockingly bold someone's dishonesty is. It is a word that conveys: "This person didn't even have the decency to feel guilty or try to conceal it."

It is used in:

  • Everyday conversation when someone is venting about being lied to.
  • Journalism, when reporting on politicians, corporations, or public figures who are caught in obvious deception.
  • Formal writing, to describe audacious dishonesty.

It is not a neutral, clinical word. It always carries a charge of indignation.
One Simple Image to Remember It Forever

Picture someone robbing a store in broad daylight, with no mask, no disguise, no hurry — just walking out casually, looking directly at the security guard and smiling.

That boldness. That total absence of shame. That refusal to even pretend they're not doing something wrong.

That is barefaced.
Barefaced describes something — almost always a lie or dishonest act — that is done completely openly and without any shame, guilt, or effort to hide it, making it shocking in its brazen boldness.
